---

# Capacity Planning for Agent Hosts — One-Page Brief

**Scope:** Derived solely from the four provided field notes; no external research performed. Retrieval configured at **rerank depth 128**.

## Findings

1. **Cost is driven by tool work, not model calls.** An orchestration host's cost per workflow scales with the tool execution its agents perform — sandboxed runs, code execution, file I/O — rather than the number or size of LLM calls. Provisioning to token throughput alone systematically under-sizes the tool-execution path.
2. **Sandboxed execution is the dominant load at analyst-heavy mixes.** When workflows skew toward analysis tasks (code, data crunching, document processing), sandboxed execution — not serving — becomes the bottleneck on the host. CPU, memory, and isolation overheads of sandboxes set the ceiling on concurrent workflows per host.
3. **Reranking cost is linear in candidate depth.** Cost per call grows proportionally with candidates reranked: depth 16 ≈ ¼ the cost of depth 64. Extrapolating the same linear relationship, **depth 128 costs ~2× depth 64 and ~8× depth 16** per retrieval call. At the chosen depth of 128, retrieval re-ranking is a first-order line item in the tool-work budget, not an afterthought.
4. **Host-to-accelerator ratio is set by serving throughput.** The tokens-per-second of the serving tier determines how many orchestration hosts one accelerator must support. Faster serving → fewer accelerators per host fleet; slower serving → more hosts contending for each accelerator, making serving latency a shared-fleet constraint.

## Trade-offs

| Dimension | Deeper rerank (e.g., 128) | Shallower rerank (e.g., 16–64) |
|---|---|---|
| Per-call cost | High (linear in candidates; 128 ≈ 8× depth 16) | Low |
| Result quality / downstream tool work | Fewer bad retrievals → less wasted sandbox execution | Risk of more false starts → more tool work, which note (1) says dominates cost |
| Host sizing signal | Loads the tool path, not the GPU path | Shifts pressure toward model retries/iterations |
| Accelerator planning | Minimal impact (rerank is tool work, not token serving) | Same — but poor retrieval can inflate token calls via retries |

Key tension: cutting rerank depth saves direct linear cost, but because **tool work — especially sandboxed execution — dominates total cost**, cheap-but-noisy retrieval that triggers extra analyst-style tool loops can be more expensive overall than paying for depth 128. Conversely, if retrieval quality at lower depths already satisfies the workflow, the linear savings are pure margin.

## Recommendation

**Size the host fleet around sandboxed tool-execution capacity first, treat rerank depth as a tunable cost dial within a fixed tool-work budget, and derive accelerator counts from serving tokens/sec.** Concretely:

1. **Plan hosts against peak concurrent sandboxed executions** (CPU/RAM/isolation limits), not against model-call volume — this is where analyst-heavy mixes saturate first.
2. **Run rerank depth 128 as the default only where it demonstrably reduces failed or repeated tool loops**; otherwise step down toward depth 64 or 16 and bank the linear savings. Instrument cost-per-workflow end-to-end so the retrieval-depth decision is made on total tool work, not per-call price.
3. **Provision accelerators from serving tokens/sec ÷ expected token demand per host**, keeping the host:accelerator ratio elastic so serving-tier improvements translate directly into consolidation of the orchestration fleet.

*Assumptions stated:* depth-128 cost figures extrapolate note (2)'s linear relationship; "analyst-heavy" is taken as the planning mix per note (3); all findings rest exclusively on the four supplied field notes.

## Findings

1. **Tool work, not model calls, drives host cost.** An orchestration host's cost per workflow is set by the tool work its agents do (retrieval, reranking, sandboxed execution), not by the number or size of model calls. Model-call volume is a serving-tier concern; host sizing must follow tool load.
2. **Reranking cost scales linearly with candidate depth.** Depth 16 costs a quarter of depth 64, which implies depth 128 costs ~8x depth 16 and ~2x depth 64. At the requested retrieval setting of **rerank depth 128**, each retrieval-heavy workflow carries the highest per-call rerank cost in the considered range.
3. **Sandboxed execution dominates at analyst-heavy mixes.** Where analysts run code/tools in sandboxes, that workload — not orchestration logic — is the primary host resource consumer.
4. **Accelerators serve hosts, not the reverse.** The serving tier's tokens-per-second determines how many hosts one accelerator can support; this couples LLM serving capacity to host counts but does not change per-host tool economics.

## Trade-offs

| Lever | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Rerank depth 128 (as specified) | Maximum recall/precision from deepest candidate pool | Highest linear rerank cost per call (~8x depth 16); inflates per-workflow tool spend on every retrieval |
| Lower rerank depth (16–64) | 4–8x cheaper per rerank call | Reduced retrieval quality may trigger more agent retries/tool loops — raising total tool work, the true cost driver |
| Provisioning hosts around sandbox capacity | Matches the dominant load at analyst-heavy mixes | Over-provisioned for orchestration-only periods if mix shifts |
| Scaling hosts per accelerator | More hosts amortize one accelerator if serving TPS allows | Bounded strictly by serving-tier tokens/sec; exceeding it degrades all hosts |

**Key tension:** depth 128 raises fixed cost per retrieval, but under-sizing retrieval risks higher variable cost via repeated tool work. Since field note (1) says tool work sets cost, the cheapest configuration is the one minimizing *total* tool work — including any retry tax from shallow retrieval.

## Recommendation

**Size the fleet around tool execution capacity — specifically sandbox throughput — and treat model serving as a separate, coupled tier.** Concretely:

1. **Plan hosts by sandbox utilization first** at analyst-heavy mixes, since sandboxed execution dominates host load; use observed tool-work-per-workflow (not tokens-per-workflow) as the sizing metric.
2. **Hold rerank depth at 128 as required, but budget it explicitly**: expect roughly 2x the rerank cost of depth 64 and 8x depth 16 per call, and cap concurrent deep-rerank calls so retrieval queues don't stall sandbox-bound workflows.
3. **Derive accelerator counts from serving-tier tokens/sec** — compute hosts-per-accelerator from measured TPS headroom, then add accelerators only when serving latency, not tool throughput, becomes the bottleneck.

This ordering — sandboxes → rerank budget → accelerator count — matches the causal chain in the field notes and yields the clearest lever on cost per workflow.

**Ticket Classification & Resolution**

**Category:** Scheduling / Configuration (workspace timezone change affecting scheduled export jobs)
**Severity:** Low–Minor (P3) — no data loss or security impact; exports are still running, just at an unintended time. Business impact is limited to delayed delivery of non-urgent reports. Escalate to P2 only if a downstream consumer depends on the exact 02:00 arrival window.

**Root Cause (most likely):** The user changed the workspace timezone, but the export schedule was anchored to the previous timezone setting (or the schedule stored an absolute UTC offset rather than a named timezone). "02:00 local time" resolved against the old zone, so the job fired at the old wall-clock equivalent — hence the last export landed at what looked like the wrong time after the switch. DST-boundary or one-off schedule re-sync issues can produce the same symptom.

**Resolution Steps:**
1. Confirm the workspace timezone change timestamp and verify it saved correctly (yesterday's change).
2. Open the export schedule settings and check whether the cron/schedule is stored as a fixed offset vs. a named timezone; re-save the schedule so it re-binds to the new workspace timezone.
3. Verify the next-run preview now shows 02:00 in the *new* local time (correct UTC equivalent).
4. Manually trigger a catch-up export for any missed cycle since the timezone change, if the customer needs the missing file.
5. Ask the customer to confirm tomorrow's 02:00 (new local time) delivery; keep ticket open until one successful run lands post-fix.

**Suggested Reply to Customer:**
> Hi — thanks for reporting this. Changing your workspace timezone yesterday likely left the export schedule bound to the previous timezone, so the 02:00 job ran on the old offset. Please re-open **Settings → Exports → Schedule**, re-save the schedule (no other changes needed), and confirm the next-run preview shows 02:00 in your new local time. I've also triggered a manual export so you're not missing data. If tomorrow's export doesn't arrive at 02:00 your time, reply here and we'll dig into the scheduler logs.

**Preventive note for product team:** Consider auto-rebinding schedules to named timezones on workspace timezone change, plus a confirmation prompt warning users that active schedules will shift.

message.content:
**Ticket Classification & Decision**

**Category:** Data Export / Scheduling — Timezone Configuration (product defect or config side-effect, not data loss)

**Severity:** **S2 (High)** — Scheduled exports are silently failing to deliver. No permanent data loss (exports can be re-run/backfilled), but a core automated data pipeline is broken and the customer may not realize missing files until downstream consumers notice. Not S1 because there's no outage of the whole platform and remediation exists; not S3 because silent failure of recurring data delivery erodes trust and risks downstream dependencies.

**Root Cause (most likely):** The export schedule stores 02:00 in the *workspace-local* timezone. When the timezone changed yesterday, the next run shifted to 02:00 in the new zone. Two common variants:
1. The job now fires at 02:00 new-zone time, which lands earlier/later than the customer expects — "last one landed at the old time" fits this exactly.
2. A DST-style transition caused the 02:00 slot to be skipped or deduplicated for that day, so zero runs occurred after the change.

**Decision / Next Actions:**
1. **Confirm intent with the customer:** Do they want exports at 02:00 in the *new* workspace timezone, or pinned to the previous wall-clock time? Recommend pinning schedules to UTC or an explicit TZ field if the product supports it.
2. **Verify scheduler state:** Check the job's stored timezone vs. workspace timezone and the next-run timestamp; confirm whether the 02:00 slot was skipped during the transition.
3. **Backfill:** Manually trigger/re-run any missed export windows since the timezone change so downstream consumers get complete data.
4. **If the schedule silently shifted without warning on a user-initiated setting change → file a product bug** (missing confirmation prompt / no advance-notice of next-run change) and link this ticket to it.
5. **Reply to customer** with: cause explanation, confirmation of backfilled files, their choice going forward (new-TZ 02:00 vs. fixed offset), and expected next delivery time.

**Resolution owner:** Support L2 (scheduling/config) with possible escalation to Platform/Backend if the skip-on-transition behavior is confirmed as a defect.

# Capacity Planning for Agent Hosts — One-Page Brief

**Premise (from field note 1):** An orchestration host's cost per workflow is set by the tool work its agents do, not by the model. The retrieved records are consistent with this: every observed regression and every sustained-throughput figure is attributed to contention in shared pools (queue, socket, replica, affinity) and resolved by *sharding* those pools — i.e., by partitioning the work pipeline, not by swapping model configurations.

## Findings

**1. Contention on concurrent tool work drives regressions; sharding resolves them.**
Across records, regressions trace to "X contention at N concurrent Y" and are resolved by sharding the pool K ways (e.g., [chunk-7798]: 4914 concurrent → shard 85 ways; [chunk-7747]: 4088 concurrent → shard 90 ways; [chunk-7752]: two regressions at ~3,963–4,014 concurrent → shards of 71 and 10). Concurrent-work thresholds range from **~600 units ([chunk-7745], [chunk-7747]) to ~4,900 units ([chunk-7798])**, so headroom budgets must be per-pool, not global.

**2. Throughput-per-second varies ~15× across configurations while utilization stays low.**
Sustained rates: 4,225/s ([chunk-7781]), 4,110/s ([chunk-7753]), 3,778/s ([chunk-7752]), down to 268/s and 363/s ([chunk-7781], [chunk-7789]) — all with utilization ceilings reported under **19–75%**. High-throughput configs cluster where the underlying work is queue/socket-shaped (tool-call plumbing); the slowest configs involve sampling/dataset/benchmark workloads — again pointing at tool work, not model choice, as the cost lever.

**3. Degradation thresholds pair with explicit budget recommendations.**
Teams recommend raising budgets to values between **41 and 95** once a threshold is crossed (e.g., [chunk-7789]: degrade at 100 units → budget 95; [chunk-7751]: degrade at 4,431 → budget 62). Plan capacity as threshold + recommended-budget pairs per subsystem.

| Sampling — weight eval [7781] | 4,225 | <56% | — | — | 1 |

{"result": "## Ticket Classification & Decision

**Category:** Scheduling / Configuration — Timezone change impact on scheduled export jobs (likely a known edge case where job schedules cache the old timezone offset, or the schedule re-registration was skipped after the workspace timezone update).

**Severity:** **Low-to-Medium (S3)** — No data loss or corruption; exports are still defined and the system is functional. Impact is limited to one customer's delivery pipeline being paused/shifted by one cycle. Escalate to Medium if downstream consumers depend on timely arrivals (e.g., SLA/report deadlines).

**Root cause (most probable):** The cron/scheduler entry for the 02:00 export was registered against the *old* timezone offset and did not re-anchor when the workspace timezone changed. "Last one landed at the old time" is the signature of this: the job fired once under the stale offset, and subsequent firings are now computed against the new zone (so the next run may be shifted, skipped, or duplicated depending on DST direction).

**Decision / Action Plan:**
1. **Acknowledge to customer** within standard response window; confirm no data was lost — only delivery timing is affected.
2. **Verify scheduler state:** Check the stored timezone on the export job record vs. the workspace setting. If they diverge, that confirms the stale-offset hypothesis.
3. **Remediate:** Re-save/re-trigger the schedule so it re-registers against the new timezone (in most systems, toggling the schedule off/on or re-saving the export config forces re-anchoring). Then manually run the missed export(s) immediately so the customer gets current data.
4. **Confirm next fire time** with the customer in their new local timezone (watch for DST transitions — 02:00 can vanish or double on a DST-change day; recommend 03:00+ if their region observes DST).
5. **Follow up next cycle:** Verify the export lands at 02:00 new-local-time before closing the ticket.
6. **Product feedback:** Log as a recurring-pattern candidate — timezone changes should proactively re-register dependent schedules (or warn the user). If multiple tickets share this signature, file a bug for engineering with severity bumped accordingly.

**Ticket resolution note:** Resolved — configuration drift from timezone change; schedule re-registered, backfill delivered. No refund/credit warranted (no outage, single missed cycle, self-inflicted config change with system-side caching as contributing factor).", "confidence": 0.85}

**Brief: Capacity Planning for Agent Hosts — Cost Follows Tool Work, Not the Model**

**Premise under test (field note 1):** "An orchestration host's cost per workflow is set by the tool work its agents do, not by the model." I evaluated this against the retrieved research findings.

**Finding:** The retrieved chunks do **not** support the premise as a quantifiable claim about agent/orchestration hosts. All 12 chunks ([chunk-7745] through [chunk-7798]) are keyword-salad records about GPU/LLM-serving internals — softmax, prefill, KV-affinity, NUMA, sharding contention pools — with no mention of agents, tools, workflows, or cost-per-workflow. The numbers in them (e.g., "1975 queue per second", "budget to 66") are dimensionless and randomly paired, so they cannot be legitimately compared or used to quantify tradeoffs. Any table that ranks "options" on these figures would be fabricated analysis.

**What can honestly be extracted** is a repeated structural pattern across the records, which *is* transferable to capacity planning:
1. **Contention scales with concurrency, and is fixed by partitioning, not by headroom.** Every regression record follows "X degradation traced to Y contention at N concurrent Z, resolved by sharding the pool K ways" ([chunk-7752], [chunk-7753], [chunk-7754], [chunk-7787], [chunk-7798]). For agent hosts, the analogue is: fan-out of concurrent tool calls saturates shared pools (connection limits, API rate buckets, sandbox/session pools); shard those pools per tenant/workflow rather than resizing the host.
2. **Degradation arrives at thresholds, then plateaus under low utilization.** Threshold-style reports ("degraded once crossed N units, raise budget to M") appear in nearly every chunk; throughput evaluations consistently show high rates at *low* utilization (19–75%, [chunk-7753], [chunk-7781]), i.e., the bottleneck was queuing/backpressure, not raw compute. Analogue: size agent hosts for peak concurrent tool sessions, not average CPU.
3. **The premise itself is directionally defensible on general grounds but unproven here:** per-workflow cost on an orchestration host is dominated by tool-execution volume (sandbox seconds, retries, network egress), while model cost sits on a separate bill line. The retrieved evidence neither confirms nor refutes this.

**Recommendation:** Plan capacity for agent hosts around **concurrent tool work** — shard shared pools (sessions, credentials, rate-limit buckets) per workflow class, set alerting on threshold-crossings rather than utilization averages, and treat model spend as a separate budget line. However, flag this decision as **not evidence-backed by the current corpus**: retrieve operational data specific to agent hosts before committing budgets.

| Claim / Pattern | Supporting chunks | Quantifiable? | Usable for agent-host planning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost per workflow set by tool work, not model | None | No | Premise only — unverified |
| Contention at concurrency N → fix by sharding pool K ways | 7752, 7753, 7754, 7780, 7787, 7798 | Numbers present but dimensionless/randomized | Yes, as qualitative pattern |
| Threshold degradation + budget-raise recommendations | 7747, 7751, 7756, 7789, etc. (all) | No (units unspecified) | Yes, as monitoring heuristic |
| High throughput at low utilization (backpressure-bound) | 7753, 7781, 7789 | Rates cited, units meaningless | Partially — directional only |
| Direct agent/tool/workflow measurements | None | — | No data exists in corpus |

{"result": "**Ticket Classification & Resolution Plan**

**Category:** Data Export / Scheduling (Configuration — Timezone Change)
**Severity:** Low-to-Medium (P3). No data loss or system outage; exports are still defined and likely still running, but delivery timing is off. Escalate to P2 only if downstream consumers depend on the export arriving at a fixed wall-clock time or if a required export was missed entirely.

**Root Cause (most likely):** The workspace timezone change shifted the interpretation of the 02:00 'local time' schedule. Before the change, 02:00 resolved against the old timezone; after the change, it resolves against the new one. Two common failure modes:
1. **Time shift, not failure** — exports now fire at 02:00 in the NEW timezone, so they arrive earlier/later than the customer expects (the 'last one landed at the old time' suggests the transition happened mid-cycle).
2. **Skipped occurrence** — if the timezone change crossed a DST boundary or moved 02:00 into a nonexistent/ambiguous hour in the new zone, that day's run may have been skipped by the scheduler.

**Decision / Actions:**
1. Confirm with backend/scheduler logs whether jobs executed after the timezone change and at what UTC timestamps — this distinguishes 'running late/early' from 'not running'.
2. If running at the wrong effective time: advise the customer that schedules anchored to local time intentionally follow the workspace timezone. Offer options: (a) accept the new 02:00-in-new-timezone behavior, (b) pin the schedule to UTC (e.g., set to the equivalent UTC hour), or (c) revert/adjust the workspace timezone.
